title: Mohnish Pabrai's session with EO Gurgaon on January 10, 2023
summary: Speaking to Indian entrepreneurs, Pabrai argues that business leaders are natural investors and offers capital-allocation frameworks: demand 20-25% returns on incremental capital, avoid leverage, use index funds as a fallback, plant tiny 'seed' bets in new businesses, and accept that control is overrated. He tells his own TransTech and 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' story, the Patel motel case, the Reysas (Turkey) investment, Rakesh Jhunjhunwala's Titan holding, Indian asset managers, Munger's reciprocation model, and the industrial-psychologist 'owner's manual' that confirmed investing was his calling.

ideas.idea: Entrepreneurs are already wired to be great investors because the 3-4% of time they spend on strategy uses the same brain cells as picking businesses to buy.
ideas.detail: He quotes Buffett: 'I'm a better investor because I'm a businessman, and a better businessman because I'm an investor.' Buffett took that 4% strategy slice and expanded it to 80% of his time by making passive investments instead of doing the heavy lifting.

ideas.idea: Capitalism is creative destruction: almost every business created will eventually disappear, and any good mousetrap attracts competition that erodes its advantage.
ideas.detail: Very few businesses from 100 years ago survive and almost none from 200-300 years ago; he cites a 700-year-old 40-room family hotel in northern Japan as the rare exception. Enduring brands like Coca-Cola, American Express, Pepsi and Visa are largely accidents of history.

ideas.idea: Do not reinvest in your business unless incremental capital earns at least 20-25%; if you invest 20 crores you should see 4-5 crores come out.
ideas.detail: Cement companies are on a treadmill of building plants that project low teens returns and may deliver 9%; entrepreneurs are optimists and should discount their own projections. Needing lots of leverage to make the numbers work is a red flag, since great businesses earn high ROE without leverage.

ideas.idea: If your business cannot compound capital well, treat it as a cash cow and put the cash into a low-cost mid-cap or small-cap index fund.
ideas.detail: This gets double-digit returns with little work and rupee-cost averaging over time reduces risk.

ideas.idea: Plant new seeds with tiny bets in adjacent businesses and treat the small invested capital as a tuition bill.
ideas.detail: Because payoffs are asymmetric (max loss is 1x, upside can be 10-100x), serial small bets are worth pursuing; once a second engine works, shift the accelerator to whichever has better returns on capital. The Reysas father-son team does exactly this with $0.5-1 million bets.

ideas.idea: Control is overrated; the market, competitors, customers and employees control you anyway, and the best position is passive investor.
ideas.detail: Buffett never controlled Coca-Cola yet gets 1-2 cents from every eighth can opened; Pabrai's job at Reysas is just to cheer them on, meet once a year, and not sit on the board. 'If you don't have any employees, you have no problems.'

ideas.idea: Part-time investing turned $1 million into $13 million from 1995 to 2000, outearning his 70-80 person IT company in some years, which pushed him into full-time investing.
ideas.detail: He spent 10-20 hours a week studying businesses after reading about Buffett in 1994. His two rules: if you are not excited to go to work on Monday, don't go; and hit the reset button. His YPO forum suggested owning the business without running it, and the new CEO sold TransTech within months.

ideas.idea: Auction-driven public markets overshoot and undershoot far more than the underlying asset changes, and that mispricing is what pays the bills.
ideas.detail: A 10-crore Gurgaon apartment is quoted at 10 crores every day by a broker, but if listed its market cap would swing from 60 to 120 crores over a year; you can sometimes buy 100 crores of assets for 70 crores.

ideas.idea: Entrepreneurs do not take risk; they do everything to minimize it, and 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' was how TransTech was started.
ideas.detail: He worked on the startup for 9-10 months before quitting at 25, with clients and cash flow already exceeding his salary; the downside was $30,000 of 401k and $70,000 of credit card debt that US bankruptcy law would wipe, and his bosses promised him his job back with a raise. Both later became Pabrai Funds investors.

ideas.idea: The Patels are the classic Dhandho case: 0.1% of the US population now controls 70-75% of US motels, built from nothing by being the lowest-cost operator.
ideas.detail: Refugees from Uganda moved into motels, replaced staff with family, cooked vegetarian meals at home, undercut $35 rooms at $32, and used non-recourse leverage to buy the next motel for a cousin. When the book came out ~15 years ago the figure was 40%; now they own Hiltons and Marriotts too.

ideas.idea: Business biographies are his favorite genre, and he is currently reading Roy Thomson of Fleet Street.
ideas.detail: Thomson went broke and ended up owning some 300 newspapers and TV stations; Pabrai tripled the size of his library after moving to Austin about a year earlier. He also praised the Hero Honda family book as a classic Dhandho story.

ideas.idea: Reysas in Turkey was bought at a $20 million market cap against roughly $800 million of liquidation value, a once-in-a-lifetime mispricing.
ideas.detail: 12 million square feet of warehouses 99% leased to Amazon, Ikea and Carrefour on inflation-indexed or dollar leases, worth ~$1 billion at $80/sq ft with $200 million of debt; plus Turkey's largest freight rail network, 2,000 trucks, forklift rental and vehicle inspection businesses. For $7 million he got a third of the company; the stock is now $350-400 million in dollars despite the lira collapse and still undervalued.

ideas.idea: Turkey is a dream market because locals 'play the market', with the free float turning over every nine days, transferring wealth from the active to the inactive.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: High inflation, a collapsing currency and departed foreign investors made it optically cheap when he began visiting in 2018-2019 with a local Buffett/Graham disciple friend; he quotes Buffett that the stock market transfers wealth from the active to the inactive.

ideas.idea: The Reysas founder's only test is how quickly a dollar invested comes back; if not within two to three years in dollars, he is not interested.
ideas.detail: The father never went to college and does not know the term return on equity, yet reinvests at 25-35% returns; Pabrai will not sell at $1 billion and intends to leave them alone for 20 years, targeting $5 billion.

ideas.idea: You only need one Reysas, not ten; his 2023 resolution is to deeply study 50 businesses in hopes of finding one.
ideas.detail: Most candidates are discarded in five minutes; only those with high ROE, a runway and great management that survive two or three hours of screening count toward the 50. By January 10 he had studied and rejected one.

ideas.idea: Idea sourcing needs no team: 13F filings in the US and public disclosure of what great Indian investors like RK Damani own feed the hopper.
ideas.detail: He can see what Buffett bought last quarter and what many great investors have bought, then study those; RK Damani owns VST Industries, a tobacco company.

ideas.idea: Indian wealth and asset management has such a long runway that he could pay 20x earnings and still do well, because household savings are shifting from mattresses, gold and real estate into financial assets.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: The business needs no capital, has high ROE, and assets stick to the brand: when IIFL hired senior Kotak wealth managers they brought only 15% of their assets while 85% stayed with Kotak. He suggests a basket of the listed fund houses, letting Raamdeo Agrawal run it, and not touching it for 20-30 years.

ideas.idea: He never has a view on markets or recessions; forecasting 500 businesses is a fool's errand when even one business's trajectory is hard to call.
ideas.detail: Nobody foresaw the Ukraine invasion at the start of 2022 and COVID is still around three years on; macro noise is irrelevant to whether a specific company like Kapoor Watches engages its customers over the next 1-5 years. India likely does well given its tailwinds, but he doesn't invest on that basis.

ideas.idea: Indian families can now send money abroad and putting about a fourth of family wealth into a low-cost S&P 500 index fund is a good, low-effort choice.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: At about 10 basis points a year you own Amazon, Microsoft, Salesforce and other businesses with long runways; averaging in over time makes a 5-10% market drop irrelevant.

ideas.idea: You don't need to be right often; wait for the seven moons to line up and swing hard, as Rakesh Jhunjhunwala did with Titan.
ideas.detail: Jhunjhunwala traded rapidly on four screens yet held Titan untouched for 25+ years; it grew from ~4% of his portfolio to a multi-billion-dollar position that would have been half his wealth even if the other 96% went to zero. He loved the Tatas' governance and just did nothing.

ideas.idea: Poor Charlie's Almanack is the best book in his library, better than a college education, and he rereads it every year.
ideas.detail: Munger's Psychology of Human Misjudgement speech distills 50 years of experience into an hour of reading; understanding and overlaying the ~25 mental models gives a huge advantage in business, career and personal life.

ideas.idea: Reciprocation is hardwired but uncalibrated, so small favors create disproportionate goodwill; he exploits this by mailing prospective investors a package with a $50 pen and books.
ideas.detail: The brain evolved reciprocation from sharing kills in small groups but cannot remember the size of a favor; only about 1 in 200 return the package, and the minimum investment to reciprocate is $3 million. You want large parts of the world to feel they owe you something.

ideas.idea: Everyone should get an 'owner's manual' from industrial psychologists, as he did in 1999, to discover who they really are rather than following prescribed paths.
ideas.detail: A 360 assessment through his YPO forum showed he is a solo game player who likes games with odds in his favor and had no business running a 200-person IT company; the psychologists endorsed the yet-to-launch Pabrai Funds and one invested $100,000. He rereads the report annually, recommends Jack Skeen, and says kids should do it at 18.
